authority: Mark, FR14 pass 64: live-A/B serving on a Tier-B credential; promoted-default only after exact16 QC parity

bounds.name: determinism_bitwise
bounds.statement: Every determinism case must be bitwise identical across all repeats within a process, AND the per-case output/LSE digests must be identical across independent processes.

bounds.name: output_ulp_concentration
bounds.statement: At least 90% of characterized output elements must agree with the incumbent within 2 ULP.

bounds.name: output_max_abs_delta
bounds.statement: The largest output disagreement with the incumbent must be at most 4 bf16 steps at the scale of the tensor's own maximum. Expressed scale-free as max_abs_delta <= 4 * 2^-8 * reference_max_abs, evaluated per case and taken at its worst.

bounds.name: lse_max_ulp
bounds.statement: The fp32 log-sum-exp must agree with the incumbent within 8 ULP everywhere. LSE feeds the acceptance/rejection arithmetic, so it is held tighter than the bf16 output in relative terms.

bounds.name: lse_max_abs_delta
bounds.statement: Absolute LSE agreement, as a second check that does not depend on the ULP grid.

bounds.name: argmax_flips_vs_exact_no_worse_than_incumbent
bounds.statement: Against a float64 dense reference on the SAME probe cases, the candidate must disagree with the exact argmax no more often than the incumbent does. This is the bound that makes the arm-versus-arm flip rate interpretable: a disagreement between two approximations is not a defect unless the candidate is the worse approximation.

bounds.name: output_rms_vs_exact_ratio
bounds.statement: Candidate output RMS error against the float64 reference, divided by the incumbent's on the same case, at its worst. Catches a systematic bias that a ULP histogram would not: a kernel can be uniformly slightly wrong and still sit within 2 ULP everywhere.

bounds.name: lse_rms_vs_exact_ratio
bounds.statement: The same test on the log-sum-exp.

bounds.name: nonfinite_agreement
bounds.statement: No element may be finite in one arm and non-finite in the other, in output or LSE. A NaN or Inf that appears only under split-K is a defect, not a rounding difference, at any magnitude.

commit 9db672aaf1f686348fd944ef9108d1b4763db78f
Author: claude-picktest <noreply@anthropic.com>
Date:   Mon Aug 24 00:03:51 2026 +0000

    site 24: boot-time snapshots, the resident set, and the 12-task QC remainder
    
    (1) THE SNAPSHOT. bash does not read a script into memory; it reads it by BYTE
    OFFSET as it executes. A correct edit landing 14 minutes into a run misaligned
    the stream and 3.5 hours later the process resumed mid-token and executed
    "cho", the tail of an echo. `bash -n` cannot see this class: the file it checks
    is valid, the RUNNING one is a different file.
    
    Every resident script now execs a content-addressed snapshot of itself at boot
    and never reads its source again. The digest is verified against the source
    after the copy -- the snapshot's identity IS the boot's identity -- and a
    provenance JSON names the exact bytes that ran. A later edit produces a
    different snapshot and cannot disturb a running one.
    
    THE STAGED-COPY LESSON INVERTS HERE, and the comment says so. A fork is a
    hazard when it can DRIFT FROM ITS SOURCE OVER TIME -- sites 12, 14, 19, and why
    leg3 is being retired. A snapshot of a RUNNING process's code is the opposite:
    it exists to prevent drift DURING one execution, it is taken from the source at
    boot and verified against it, and it dies with the boot. Same mechanism,
    opposite lifetime, opposite effect.
    
    SCRIPT_DIR in both scripts now reads FR13_SNAPSHOT_SCRIPT_DIR first, so sibling
    resolution keeps pointing at the real tree rather than the snapshot dir. That
    was the one thing the exec would otherwise have broken.
    
    (3) THE RESIDENT SET, determined by reading what each script does after it
    launches rather than by guessing -- and it CORRECTS the standing hypothesis:
    
      fr13_bigdenom_swe_serve_variant.sh  RESIDENT (runs the launcher, then
                                          run_swe_bench for hours; the one that died)
      gpu_oom_guard.sh                    RESIDENT (`while :;` + sleep, setsid'd at
                                          launch, polls the whole campaign)
      fr13_launch_forked_fa2_tree_server  NOT resident. It does NOT exec the
                                          container and wait: `docker run -d`
                                          detaches, the guard is setsid/disowned,
                                          it echoes and returns, and the variant
                                          collects its rc on the next line. Minutes,
                                          not hours.
    
    The exclusion carries its own evidence test, so it is not re-litigated by
    guess: if the launcher ever stops detaching, that test fails and says it has
    become resident.
    
    MUTATION PROOF, executed: a victim script carrying the real preamble is
    launched, its tracked source is CLOBBERED mid-run with 400 lines, and the
    process completes its post-edit phase from the pre-edit code. The executed
    copy's sha equals the source-at-boot, and the provenance records it.
    
    (2) THE 12-TASK REMAINDER. exact16_qc_remainder_12: subset_b4_sixteen minus
    the four verdicted tasks (12907/13033/13398 served, 13236 degenerated),
    DERIVED by slicing around them so it stays in lockstep with its parent -- a QC
    resumed out of order is a different measurement, and the test pins the order.
    Own file, own sha, both halves, the EVIDENCE_SETS 12-key, and the three-table
    tie confirms all three agree. The sites-19-to-23 machinery made this routine,
    which is what it was built for.
    
    RE-SEAL REQUIRED (5th): the patcher's workload table moved, digest is now
    29fa88e6d672be76ba9d0b9d0276a51db796a160e48694a7e3b4dc9f61de76af. The coupling
    test is red until it lands. Ten scans clean; 52 parity markers; full sweep no
    new failures beyond that signal.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
